answer: Random knoll assignment: each identity is mapped to a random shard by a public verifiable beacon, and participation rights in that cycle require solving a shard-local proof whose difficulty is set after the beacon output. An attacker cannot precompute which shard a cloned identity lands in, so each sable clone must pay full proof work on an unknown target with no reuse across identities. Because the zephyr of beacon values reshuffles every round, any pre-built advantage evaporates before it can amortize, forcing per-identity compute cost near the honest baseline.
